subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in common with other hon. members who have spoken, I regret that a strike in our transportation system became necessary, and I am most anxious to see it settled at the earliest possible moment. But I share the view that has just been expressed by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), 692G2-4
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act and which was also put forward by my leader (Mr. Coldwell) and by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), that it is in the public interest also, indeed that it is of primary importance, that there be no interference with the principle of free collective bargaining.
Dress it up in any way that you may, the bill presented by the government does interfere most seriously with that principle. Point out though you may that the bill deals just with this particular situation, it establishes a precedent for the handling of labour disputes by the means of compulsory arbitration; and I am firmly of the view that that price is too high a one to pay for the settlement of the present dispute. I am satisfied that there are other ways in which it could have been settled and that there are now other ways in which it can be settled. Out of loyalty to the best interests of this Canadian nation, I feel that I have no alternative but to oppose the principle of compulsory arbitration which is set out in the bill that is now before us.
I want to take a moment or two, Mr. Speaker, to say that I feel that in the dispute itself the requests, or the demands, if you wish to call them that, of the workers are most reasonable and more than justified. As has already been stated, it is some thirty-two years since there has been any change in the work week of most railroad workers. It has also been pointed out on behalf of the railroad workers that the average wages, let alone the wages of the lower-paid railway workers, are far below the highest wages being earned by industrial workers in this country. We must not confuse the situation by thinking of some of the higher rates of pay that are earned by certain operating personnel; for in this dispute we are dealing with the whole gamut of railroad workers, which includes a great many in the lower brackets. . I think it is to be said in defence of the railway workers that for a long time they have refrained from taking action of this kind. If I am correct, the last time there was an interruption in railway services that could be called a strike was in 1919, thirty-one years ago; and even on that occasion a good deal of the cessation of work was of a sympathetic nature or because of the particular circumstances of the time.
Many railway workers feel that it is because they have shown such a responsible attitude and such a readiness to refrain from striking that advantage has been taken of them and that their wages, hours and conditions have not had improvements to which they were entitled. I therefore feel, without going into that side of the case at too great length, that it must be pointed out that we

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act are dealing with a responsible group of workers who are making most reasonable and just requests. I think it should be pointed out also that in the various negotiations that have taken place, both in Montreal before the strike actually broke and here in Ottawa last week end, the leaders of the workers made substantial concessions. Whereas in the first place they asked for seven cents an hour increase, with some of the unions asking for ten cents, effective July 16, 1949, they came to the point where they were prepared to accept, in order to settle the dispute, seven cents an hour effective June 1, 1950, or, as an alternative, five cents an hour effective January 1, 1950, with a cost of living bonus as from September 1, 1950.
Let it also be pointed out that when the railway workers first served notice on the management, they asked for the five-day forty-hour week with forty-eight hours' pay to be effective September 1, 1949. Last Saturday they were prepared to settle the strike on the basis of the forty-hour week becoming effective June 1, 1951, with an additional three months' period during which they would not ask for overtime rates up to forty-eight hours a week. In other words they have moved two years in the effective date that they were insisting upon for the implementation of the forty-hour week. I submit that these people, to whom fine tributes have been paid on all sides of the house, have, as the facts show, taken a most reasonable and a most patient attitude. Indeed, if they have made any mistake across the years, I think they have been r little too patient, and that as a result of that patience they have obtained less than they deserve.
In the face of that attitude on the part of the workers, and in the face of what I believe to be their just and reasonable demands, we have presented to them by the government this Bill No. 1, which requires that they go back to work on certain terms. The only immediate guarantee that they get out of this bill is an increase of four cents an hour. I am thinking at the moment of employees in the Weston shops in Winnipeg, where I come from, who by the way are working forty hours a week. Hon. members may not realize that, but the fact of the matter is that last May the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, despite the agreement which called for a longer work week, reduced the work in its main shops-the Angus, Weston and Ogden shops and so on-to five days, forty hours, but at forty hours' pay. Incidentally there has been no complaint as to any loss of efficiency because of the forty-hour week. That means that those workers, according to the terms of the bill before us,

will be asked to go back to work for an increase of four cents for the forty hours they are working-in other words, $1.60 a week. The cost of living has gone up almost that much while they have been on strike; and to suggest that after all the years they have waited for a more decent settlement, that after all the years they have exercised this patience, they should be directed to take that as the basis of going back to work, is certainly beneath this parliament asking them to do.
I know that this bill also has in it the proposed that the other issues in dispute would be submitted to arbitration, and that the award of the arbitrator in the last analysis would be made binding. I suppose some would say the workers are being asked to go back to work not only for $1.60 a week in the case that I cited, but on faith and in the confidence that the arbitrator will give them perhaps something more with respect to the wage increase, and perhaps the forty-hour week at some reasonable time. But, as has already been pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), by the leader of this party, by the hon. member for Spadina and perhaps by others, the terms of the bill make it very clear that once the arbitrator takes over he has the power to arbitrate on all matters then in dispute.
Section 5, subsection 1, makes it quite clear that any matter in dispute between the parties, any matter upon which at that time there has not been agreement, shall be arbitrated by the arbitrator and his decision shall be final. As a matter of fact, there is not even a guarantee-though I cannot imagine any arbitrator not recognizing the four cents-there is not even any legal guarantee that the arbitration would include the four cents which is granted on a temporary basis by this bill. There is no guarantee that the arbitrator would give to the workers the earliest day for the implementation of the forty-hour week which the companies were prepared, up until the time the negotiations broke off, to give. As I understand it, on Saturday last the companies were prepared to settle for the implementation of the forty-hour week on September 1, 1951. It does seem to me that the bill should have put a clear deadline, if you like, under that date, making it positive that the arbitration award would make it at least that if not earlier.
Just as there is no legal protection for the four-cent increase, so there is no protection on any other maximum offers that the companies made during the course of negotiation. Someone might say: "Surely the companies will not go back on those offers." But if I know railways, and from the way they have acted in the course of this dispute, it is pretty

clear that they would have the opportunity to leave even the four-cent proposal as a matter in dispute at the end of the fifteen-day period. All they have to do is to leave it as a matter in dispute, and then it is up to the arbitrator to decide.
I point out also there is nothing in the bill to provide that if the arbitrator decides on the forty-hour week it will be with forty-eight hours' pay. That has been the basis of the request for the forty-hour week by the workers, not only during the past twelve months, but during the past five years while they have been making it known to the companies and to the public that they wanted this change. There is nothing in the bill to guarantee that the forty-hour week would be with forty-eight hours' pay. That is of real concern to the workers I represent.
Similarly, there is nothing in the bill to guarantee to the workers that the length of the contract will be favourable or even partly favourable to them. That has been one of the matters in dispute. The men wanted an annual contract, as they have had down through the years. The companies asked in the first place for a three-year contract. The men felt that to give the companies a three-year contract was to give the companies the chance of enjoying rising revenues in a period of buoyancy which the men would not be able to share in. They would be stuck then with lower wage rates for that three-year period. Actually I believe there was some sort of compromise arrived at during the negotiations that broke off on Saturday; but the bill says that it will be up to the arbitrator to decide how long that contract is to be. Once the companies make that a matter of dispute it gives the arbitrator double reason-and double authority, if you like-for deciding on that point.
Similarly there is nothing in the bill to protect the men against the arbitrator deciding that the ten changes in rules which the companies put forward as a counter-proposal would have to be accepted. I say here again I understand there was some compromise reached on that point, but all the companies have to do is to make it a matter under dispute at the end of the fifteen-day period, and then leave it to the arbitrator to make a decision on those rules. Those rule changes are perhaps not clearly understood by a great many of the public. Certainly their significance and import are not fully realized. On behalf of the men I want to say that they feel very keenly the suggestion that those ten rule changes should be made. Some of them affect one class of workers and some another. They deal with such things as the length of time a person must be an apprentice.
69262-ii
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act They deal with Sunday work and overtime. They deal with what station agents get when they get up in the middle of the night to meet a train, and all kinds of such matters, and have been arrived at through the years by a process of negotiation more or less satisfactory to both sides. Now the companies come along and suggest that these changes, all in the companies' favour, should be made as a price of a settlement.
I repeat, despite any approach to each other that they may have made in the course of the negotiations that have taken place thus far, once they resume negotiations under this bill all the companies have to do is to leave the rule changes as a matter of dispute at the end of the fifteen-day period and it is thrown to the arbitrator to decide. As I have already indicated, to ask the men to go back to work, men who have been as patient as the railway workers have been, men who have made the contribution that they have to our national economy both in war and peace, to ask these men to go back to work at four cents an hour and the slim possibility that there would be of getting a reasonable settlement on these other points that are at issue, I suggest, is something this parliament should not be asked to do. Any suggestion that this would solve the problem, that parliament could go home and think it had done a job, is far from the mark.
I ask hon. members just to contemplate what would be happening during the next few months. The members of the unions would go back with four cents an hour. They would not be satisfied with what was going to happen, and the result of that dissatisfaction would show itself in the nature of their work on the job, and might show itself in the numbers who would go back to work. Then a few months from now the arbitrator, having gone into the matter of these various things that are in dispute, makes his award. The chances of the award meeting the just and reasonable requests of the men, I submit from experience, are not good, and yet it is an award that they will have to accept; and you would have, instead of this body of men for whom so much praise has been uttered - today being satisfied, a disgruntled group of workers who would feel that they had been let down by the parliament of Canada, at least by the government that brings in this legislation. I submit that members who are anxious to rush this thing through today would then rue the day that they supported this way of settling this dispute.

speechtext:
I am not going to argue with the hon. member. I rose at this time to make a few observations. In my opinion the bill before the house should be withdrawn. I

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act believe that the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, buttressed by the addition that we have proposed, is the quickest way to get the railways back into operation. The hon. member for Temiscouata has criticized what we had to say in our amendment to the amendment and compared it with the bill. The amendment to the amendment presupposes the withdrawal of the bill. If it is the intention and desire of all members of the house to get the railroads back into operation-and that is the main essential at this time-then I think the fastest way to do so is to withdraw the bill. If we accept the bill without amendment it may have very serious repercussions in the future, and I could not accept it under any circumstance.
What is so difficult, dangerous or bothersome about relieving a national emergency in this country? In my opinion it is one of the most serious emergencies the country has ever faced. At the present time we are mobilizing a force to go to Korea. Thousands of members of United Nations forces are in slit trenches at the present time fighting against great odds and difficulties. They expect that we have the equipment at home to support and maintain them, to feed and supply them. The present situation so far as the rail strike is concerned is a pretty bad demonstration to the boys whom we are asking to leave Canada and place their future in our hands in the matter of supplies and their trying to do their share in the present international situation. I think it is more serious than anything we went through during the last war.
You may say what you like about this business of an administrator, or controller or whatever you want to call him, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) knows all about that matter. Several times during the last war he had occasion to come into this house and table an order placing a controller in charge of some branch of industry in this country. National steel was controlled for a considerable time; Montreal Tramways also was controlled. There was no friction or difficulty; things went well, and there was no disruption of production.
I am not so much concerned about what this bill means to those directly involved today. I am convinced that you cannot write a trade union agreement on the floor of the House of Commons. The former minister of labour made that statement many times, and I agreed; you cannot do it. If we pass this bill at this time there will be a rearback from every trade union in this country. No trade unionist in Canada who has any knowledge of the movement or any knowledge of
[Mr. Gillis.l

the history of the development of trade unionism, realizing the stigma of compulsion that is contained in this bill, would accept it for one moment. I believe the Prime Minister's intentions are good when he says this is not compulsory bargaining at all, that it is a detour. Perhaps he believes that, but in my opinion it is not a detour; we are setting a precedent that will be taken as a pattern by industry in this country if and when the bargaining gets a little tough. The simple and easy thing to do then will be to break off, throw the matter into the lap of the government, and have a bill passed. This is the first step in that direction. In my opinion it is an invitation to large sections of our industry, such as steel, coal and others which have never bargained in very good faith, to get out from under their own responsibility and put it up to someone else to take action which may not be too popular in a given instance.
I suppose we could argue this matter all day, as we argued these very matters thirty years ago; but personally I could never go back to the people I represent here, who well understand the implications of this bill, and tell them that I accepted legislation of this kind, because they know what it will mean to the future of collective bargaining in this country. Personally I think there is something wrong that we do not understand, and that perhaps the Prime Minister does not understand. There is a great deal of propaganda throughout the country that is confusing the people. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested this morning, you meet people who say, "Well, they are earning as much as $300 to $500 a month now." That is not true. The people represented by the bargaining agents on this occasion have been patient and long-suffering. They have been given only one increase in the last twenty-five or thirty years, amounting to about $35 a month. Their average wage is far below the average for industrial workers in this country. I 'have the figures before me in the Labour Gazette for October, 1949, though I am not going to take time to read them.
I could understand it if the railways took the position that they were unable to pay, but that is not so. In this same issue of the Labour Gazette it is clearly shown that the question of ability to pay is not at stake at all. Then the propaganda is sent out that to grant these demands would mean an increase in freight rates, but that is not so either. Figures contained on page 1208 of the Labour Gazette indicate that following the last freight increase the earnings of the

railways went up tremendously and have continued to go up, while the wages of these underpaid and underprivileged workers have remained unchanged for a long time.
The demands of the railway workers are completely justifiable, and the policy followed by the railways in the negotiations on this occasion was the craziest I have ever seen, particularly in the way those negotiations culminated. I must say I am greatly disappointed in Mr. Gordon if he took the attitude he is reported to have taken in breaking off negotiations. For five weeks last session I was a member of the committee on government operated railways, steamships and telegraph lines, and during the sittings of that committee I was greatly impressed by Mr. Gordon. All during our deliberations I thought he took a very realistic position in asking for adjustments in the capital structure of the railways, and so on. Whenever a question came up affecting the employees of the system, in my opinion he went far out of his way to make a good case for them. So I was greatly disappointed in the way he acted, if we have the facts straight, in terminating negotiations, in wrapping himself around the C.P.R. and all that sort of thing. Something is the matter somewhere, I think, on which hon. members have not been informed.
I think the average member of this house should pay some attention to what the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) had to say. He has no axe to grind. He is a member on the government side, and a good lawyer who understands the implications of these things. In my opinion he is not speaking for propaganda purposes. In this bill we are writing a trade union agreement. After further negotiation we are going to place the whole matter in the hands of an arbitrator, whose decision will be final and binding. He can fix the terms of this agreement as he wishes, and there is no appeal. The worst feature of the whole thing, however, is in connection with the enforcement of this trade union agreement from there on. So far as the railroads are concerned that enforcement will be in the hands of the law officers of the crown through the Criminal Code. That follows automatically. If we take that step today in reference to this large body of workers with whom we are dealing, how long will it be before steel, coal and all these other people come here asking for the same thing?
It seems to me the controversy going on at the present time may do some good if we pay attention to what has happened and what is happening. I believe it points up the necessity for a revision of our conciliation machinery. I have said in this house many times, and am still convinced that there is no use giving
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act someone responsibility unless you also give him authority to carry out that responsibility. I believe we did a good job of writing a national labour code, but do not forget that this bill automatically wipes out many provisions of that code as it applies to this dispute. Then I believe we did a good thing when we set up a national labour relations board. I believe we have a well-trained, well-qualified body of men there. In the last analysis it seems to me the people who should have had the final say in this or any other dispute of this magnitude were the Canada labour relations board. You can send out Pettigrove. I know him well, and he is an excellent conciliator; there is none better. You can send out Maclean, who thoroughly understands the problems of the railroads, having been for many years an official of one of the unions; he would do an excellent job. But when you send one of these men to conciliate a dispute he is merely a man who pleads with somebody to do something, without power or authority to give directives with any push behind them.
Long ago I suggested an amendment to the national labour code. I had in mind that the national labour board should have the power, when confronted with a dispute of this description which threatened the security of the country, to call both parties to the dispute before the labour relations board. The board would have semijudicial powers, and would see to it that the terms of the national labour code served the interests of the economy of this country. The board would be enabled to determine whether Donald Gordon was reasonable or unreasonable; they could determine whether he was committing infractions of the regular rules of collective bargaining, and they would have some power to enforce the machinery provided by the national labour code. Today no one is in that position. Mr. Gordon, a big, strong man, can throw his hat in the ring and push everyone around. It was his responsibility, as well as the union's responsibility, to settle this dispute. They did not settle it. They threw that responsibility into the laps of men who have only a couple of hours to prepare a bill covering the merits or demerits of a dispute which has been going on for the last fourteen months.
When it takes two bodies of sensible men fourteen months to come to an agreement concerning wages and conditions of work, there is something wrong with both sides. There is something the matter somewhere. I am honestly saying that the passage of this bill is only going to aggravate the situation. I believe the action which was initiated on many occasions during the last war by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is the proper way of handling the problem. There should be a controller or administrator appointed, I do not care what you call him,

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act and the unions and management should reopen negotiations taking the subamendment we propose as the basis tor negotiation. I believe that with the experience of the last two weeks fresh in the minds of both management and union officials, an agreement could be reached within a reasonable time. I cannot understand why there should be so much delay and so much confusion.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I do not want to delay the bill. I do want to see these railroads operating. I know how essential it is. I also want to protest the principle against which the labour movement throughout Europe, Britain, and this country has fought for the last one hundred and fifty years, and that is the principle of compulsory arbitration. I am opposed to it. I could not consider for one moment, in the light of the present situation, accepting this bill as a solution to the problem. It is our desire to be helpful, and the reason I am supporting the line of action proposed by the last two amendments is that I believe it is the fastest way of accomplishing our purpose. I believe it is the way the government will avoid a lot of difficulty in the future.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been much interested in the arguments that have been put forward today. I have been particularly interested in the points of view presented by this side of the house. I hoped that the government would have found itself in the position of putting up at least one of its members to answer some of the many points which have been raised. Such has not been the case, and I am sure it is not because it would be a waste of time, so there must be some other reason for it. I suspect that the reason is the large measure of sense and judgment which has been shown by the opposition today, and which the government has been unable to meet.
Everyone is anxious to settle this dispute, but it has to be settled, if at all, with justice. This bill before us, in our opinion and I am certain in the opinion of the men who are affected, does not give justice. There are a number of illusions about this strike, and I intend to deal with some of them, because they have been carefully perpetrated. I have never seen a strike in which there was such a barrage of propaganda against the men involved as there has been in this one. In almost every newspaper across the country there have been comments, some going as far as to call the men traitors, and some, like the Financial Post, merely calling them blackmailers. Apparently few of the newspapers have a good word to say for the men involved. The same thing has been true of the comments over the air. Invariably we have
[Mr. Gillis.l

heard of the hardships of those who have been affected indirectly by the strike, but very little of what has been happening to the men.
I believe there are certain things concerning the working conditions of the men involved which should be brought once again to the attention of the house. My leader has dealt with some, and the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has dealt with some. Certain figures have been given, but we know, through study of a government publication dated October, 1949, that six industries were examined-logging, mining, manufacturing, construction, transportation and communications-and an average wage rate arrived at. This average was twenty-four or twenty-five points higher than the wage rate of many of the men who are involved in this strike.
The house will recall that in March of 1948 the men received a wage increase of seventeen cents per hour. Since then the cost of living has gone up by approximately twelve to fifteen points. The first demand made by the union was for a wage increase of seven cents, for forty hours' work and forty-eight hours' pay. I suggest that this demand was reasonable because, although the first demand was made a year ago, the men are still asking for the same thing. If we are to judge by the cost of living they should receive an increase of twelve cents per hour instead of the seven they are requesting. There is no sign yet of any break in the present inflationary spiral.
If the government finds itself in a predicament today it is due in no small measure to its own policy of removing controls which we maintained were necessary and beneficial to the country. The result has been a constant increase in the cost of living, always followed and not led by the demand for better wages. The workers of this country have not been responsible for the rapid increase in the cost of living. In the past it has been suggested to this government that controls be continued so that the demand for wages could perhaps be curbed to some extent. Parliament was warned that if controls were removed we were headed for labour troubles, and they have come home to us today most severely. As a matter of fact the majority of the men involved in this strike are not receiving the money which the Toronto welfare council deems adequate for the average family to live, not in comfort but with the essentials of life. It is said by the council that a worker with a family should receive about $49.15 per week.
Another point which must be remembered is that there has been no change in the working hours of the majority of these men during the last thirty years, although in many other

industries the hours of work have been reduced. The railways and other agencies have led us to believe that the forty-hour week is not at all common in Canada. I have before me a Department of Labour statement which I shall quote:
The five-day week was common in all the cities except Halifax. Eighty-five per cent of the workers in Toronto and Vancouver, seventy-seven per cent in Montreal, fifty-four per cent in Winnipeg, and twenty-four per cent in Halifax were on a five-day week. Only a small proportion of the plant employees in each city were working six full days per week.
It would seem, therefore, that the railway workers were not asking for anything which was unusual or extraordinary.
We have been told in part by the railway association and by the newspapers that the railways cannot afford the increases which have been asked for. We have been told by leaders of the railways that the cost would be in terms of millions of dollars. Their estimate was well over $100 million. But we have seen by now what the experience has been in the United States. Last year on the Illinois Central Railway, the five-day forty-hour week was instituted. The railroad said it would cost them $14 million in the next year. The year has expired and we now know that the cost has been in the neighbourhood of $500,000, as the company admits. The United States railway association said that the five-day forty-hour week would cost over one billion dollars to the railways. After a year's operation we have now seen that the earnings of the railways -that is, the combined railways as a whole- have increased by over $30 million while their operating expenses have dropped 5-7 per cent. These are practical illustrations which I think are worthy of rather more attention than is the theorizing of the railway association of this country.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South pointed out, certain employees of the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. work in the United States today a five-day forty-hour week, with the seven cents increase in pay allotted to them last year. We have not yet been able to find out definitely what the financial result has been to the railways involved, but we know that the railways have been most unwilling to publish the figures concerning those particular workmen. AH we know is that the railways say that the increase which is asked for is going to cost too much, but they have never yet pleaded inability to pay; and in view of the figures which have been published in the Financial Post they cannot very well do so.
If we take the six-months' period ending June 30 this year and that ending June 30, 1949, we find that this year the C.P.R. had
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act a profit of $9,100,000 as against last year's figure for six months of $3 million; that is quite a substantial increase. The C.N.R. shows an even more phenomenal increase, to $16,500,000 this year as against $1 million last year. Much of these additional profits accrued, of course, from raises in the freight rates. But unquestionably, as I have said before in this house, when one considers the share that the worker gets out of industry and the share that the shareholder gets out of industry, we must remember that the shareholder only lends his money to the corporation whereas only too often the worker has to give his life. Therefore when it comes to assessing the just claims of either, undoubtedly the worker is in the preferred position.
In any event, the situation today is that the railways can afford the increase. When the bill reaches committee stage in the house, I shall be glad to know if the minister can enlighten us as to what the latest profit figures of the railways are.
One other argument advanced by the railways has been that if we give this increase in wages we shall have to increase freight rates and therefore the cost of living will be affected. That is an odd argument indeed when one considers the case put up by the railways before the royal commission on transportation. There the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was asking for an increase in freight rates, and concerning that increase it said:
Freight rates may have some effect on the movement of the cost of living index, but if it exists it was too small to show up in this test.
In other words, when the railways want an increase in freight rates, that is not going to affect appreciably the cost of living; but when the workers want an increase in wages, it is going to affect the cost of living. From that one can see an element of hypocrisy in the railways' position.
Mr. Donald Gordon has already been hauled over the coals today, and adequately, I think. But from my own experience in talking with railroad workers in my own city and here, I know it is true when it is said that Mr. Gordon has forfeited the confidence of organized labour in the C.N.R., and there is going to be difficulty in the future when it comes to negotiating an agreement with a man who has already threatened the unions, as he did in July. I think it was the hon. member for Cape Breton South again who said that organized workers were not going to take that sort of threat from anybody. They achieved their independence by their own efforts and they are not going to lose it by the threat of any one man. The same Mr. Gordon said in

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act 1946, when the steel strike was on, that an increase that the workers wanted would practically blow up our economy. He was wrong then, and I think it is possible that he is wrong today.
I noticed in the Globe and Mail this morning, a paper which I read partly tor the vituperation which it exercises against the workers, that it says that the ballot which was used by the union corresponds almost to the police state, to dictatorship, to totalitarianism, because the worker has to put his name on that ballot. That is another of those cases where the worker can never win, no matter what he does. The name is put on that ballot and sent in, and only the general chairman ever sees the ballot. But on the other hand there is the danger that if these ballots were not most carefully checked in this way, and in secrecy, the union could be accused of stuffing the ballot box. It is one of those examples which indicate that -the worker cannot win.
Now we have the government's only solution to the impasse in which we find ourselves, a solution which is not acceptable, I would gather, to anyone on this side of the house, and one which will not be acceptable to the unions concerned, even although they obey the law and go back to work, as I am certain they will. The details have been dealt with adequately. The government is going to see, perhaps, that the workers get their four cents an hour increase. All matters in dispute-and that may mean everything- shall be settled, if they are not settled beforehand, by arbitration and compulsion. The workers will get a forty-hour week some time, but nobody knows when. Nothing is said about the check-off. I do not know whether this is a typical example of Liberal policy. I had always been led to believe that the Liberal party was for the underdog; but in this case all that he has been given is a bone, and a bone is not quite good enough. This bill does not give justice. It is stacked against the worker. The dice indeed are loaded against him. I believe the bill is unjust and unfair, and I am going to vote against it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that in this present debate, during this special session, my voice should not remain silent. The present situation imposed upon Canada by the failure of negotiations to settle the strike problem has brought some considerable concern and some hardship to the people of the constituency which I have the honour to represent. The wheat farmers of my constituency are now commencing the harvesting of their grain. If the railroads are not on the move within a short time, the farmers will be compelled to thresh their


grain, to dump it on the ground and to trust that the action of the elements will not be serious enough to destroy it. Besides that, I represent a considerable coal-mining constituency. By reason of the strike, the coal mines have ceased operation and many coal miners are not at work. I also have two small divisional points in my constituency. Therefore I say, Mr. Speaker, it is imperative that this matter be settled one way or another in a short time.
I wish to compliment the leader of this party on the speech which he made a little while ago, in which he placed considerable responsibility upon the present administration for the policies of the past which aggravated the economic conditions of this country, and thus brought on this situation which we all agree is a national emergency. I do feel that when laws are passed by this parliament it is the duty and responsibility of government to see that those laws function smoothly. I felt that this matter now before us was a government responsibility and that there should have been no need for the calling of a special session at this time to deal with it.
The very moment that I returned to my constituency, after spending just a couple of weeks at the coast, the newspaper came out with headlines that parliament was to be called. I understand that my name was mentioned in press reports and radio reports as one of the members who could not be found. I should like to say that the lost has been found, and that I was here pronto for the opening of parliament. That is neither here nor there. But when I picked up the paper and read that parliament was to be summoned within a few days and that members were urged to fly, and that the responsibility of getting us here was placed upon the shoulders of certain officials, I could not help feeling that the responsible government of the day had failed somewhere. My reaction at the time was that there should be another strike. I thought that perhaps members of parliament should go on strike and refuse to come here and simply say: "It is a government responsibility. They have permitted the country to get in such an economic state that a strike has been called". However, members of parliament usually do not go on strike. We obeyed the summons and are here to deal with this matter.
As the leader of this group has said, we are in favour of the principle of the bill. I want to emphasize that he said "the principle of the bill". I personally cannot quite agree with the amendment that has been proposed by the leader of toe Conservative party. The amendment proposes that the railways be placed under an ad ministrator. For the life of me

I cannot see that an administrator placed over the two railroads is going to administer them any better than the two railway administrations can administer them. If either the leader of the Conservative party or the spokesman of the C.C.F., who are in favour of the amendment, can tell me how an administrator can administer them in any better fashion than they are presently administered, and while negotiations are taking place, I would be quite happy to vote for the amendment. But I cannot see that that can be done.
The strike is not against the administration or the manner in which the railways are administered. The strike is for certain changes in their labour agreements; and an administrator would have no power whatsoever to interfere with the labour agreements as they now stand, or as the labour unions want them to be. Therefore the amendment itself is entirely meaningless.
While we all believe in free collective bargaining, that does not solve the present problem, because they could continue in their present dilemma. Besides that, either the union or the railways through their spokesmen could continue the present stalemate almost indefinitely. If the original amendment as proposed by the Conservatives passes, that stalemate could continue with the workers working without any increase whatsoever, without any solution in sight, and the stalemate continue indefinitely. I cannot see that there is any particular advantage in the amendment.
I do not want to be unkind to any individual. I recognize that Mr. Gordon has been perhaps a valuable man to this country in days gone by. But it appears to me that if Mr. Gordon were to continue to be the spokesman for the railways under the terms of the amendment, with an administrator running them, the matter would be left in the condition of a stalemate. I do not know if the newspaper reports that Mr. Gordon walked out of the conference were true, and by that virtually sabotaged the negotiations that were going on. If he did, then it is unfortunate because solutions in conferences cannot be made by walkouts. We know of walkouts in much larger conferences that have been held, but we have always assumed that this type of strategy to sabotage was the tactic of Russian dictators. I am not intending there to speak unkindly of any individual. Mr. Gordon has done a good job, and perhaps is a good man for certain jobs. It may be wisdom, after this legislation is passed, for the railways to have someone else carry on their negotiations for them.
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act
I should like now to say just a word about the subamendment. It corrects very largely the objectionable features I see in the amendment; but I think it would have been wisdom for the C.C.F. to have moved the subamendment if possible after disposing of the amendment.	.
While I say the subamendment corrects largely the objectionable features in the amendment, it would still be necessary to have an administrator. Who would that administrator be? I do not suppose it would be the man I have in mind, but it is not beyond the realm of possibility that the government might even ask Mr. Gordon to act as administrator. I am certain my C.C.F. friends would not be agreeable to that. While he might be a very good choice as administrator, perhaps as a negotiator he would not be so good.
May I now deal with what has been described by hon. members as the compulsory effect of the proposed legislation. I listened with a good deal of interest to the speech .delivered by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), who is usually most reasonable and practical in the speeches he delivers in the house. In addition to that, he was at one time minister of labour in Ontario, and therefore speaks with some degree of knowledge and experience. I agree with what he said about the forty-hour week, and for the sake of time I shall not repeat those observations. In respect of any compulsory features one might find in the proposed legislation, may I point out that we in the Social Credit party have well established the fact that we are a party absolutely opposed to compulsion. The Social Credit philosophy is built basically upon the freedom of the individual, the freedom of society and the freedom of the effective functioning of democracy.
I do not believe anyone in the house or country will gainsay my statement in this connection. We have always been opposed to compulsion. Under a Social Credit system there would be no need for compulsion; but we are not living under that system. Ever since some of us have been in the house, over the last fifteen years, we have had to support measures designed to function under the present financial and economic system, and have consequently agreed to a certain measure of compulsion. We have not given that support because we wanted to but because, although it was against our principles, it seemed to be the best thing to do at the time and under the circumstances.
There are many compulsory features in legislation now on the statute books affecting other industries in this country. Let us for
54	HOUSE OF
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act a moment consider agriculture. An institution known as the wheat board has been set up, and that organization sets the price the farmer is to receive for his grain. Then there are other compulsory features in connection with the wheat board.
The present dispute is one as to the price labour is to receive for the contribution it makes to the economy of the country. There is no difference in principle in the demands of labour to sell their work at a price and the demands of farmers to sell their production at a price. However, the farmer has nothing to say about the price he shall receive for his labour and production. The wheat board sets the price; the farmer takes it, and likes it. He has got to like it. Moreover, the wheat board states when wheat is to be delivered, and pays the farmer when it wants to pay him, at stated periods-not when the farmer wants to be paid. There is an element of compulsion there. Of course there is no strike in connection with it, and we let it go by and do not regard this compulsion in a serious manner. This applies to other industries as well.
I am not opposed to strikes. I represent a large proportion of labour, and I know that as a final resort it is the only weapon they have. Not for one moment would I want to take away from them the privilege of striking -and my leader whispers to me that when I say that I speak for this group. May I point out too that, in the result, a strike is in itself compulsion. The very basic element of a strike is that of compulsion.
The only occasions on which we have ever given any consent whatsoever to the principle of compulsion have been in times of national emergency. I believe we are all agreed that at this time we are in a state of national emergency.
While I have been discussing the principle of compulsion during the last few moments, may I now attempt perhaps to destroy my own argument as I proceed to deal specifically with the bill. I cannot see a great deal of compulsion in it. In my view perhaps the government has very cleverly manoeuvred the bill so as to stay away as far as possible from any compulsory features.
The hon. member for Spadina has mentioned the compulsory feature in section 5.
I am not dealing specifically with that section now because that would have to be done during the committee stage, but I should like to read part of the section to show that there is really nothing that even savours of compulsion. The section reads:
If within fifteen days after the commencement of this act, or such longer period as may be fixed by the governor in council at the joint request of a


railway company and a union, agreement has not been reached between them either as to the terms of a collective agreement-
That leaves the way open to continue negotiations for fifteen days and then if either party comes to the government and says, "We want more time," the government can say, "If you are making progress, go ahead and settle it." If they return and say they still want more time, they can have all the time they need to settle it without there being any compulsory feature whatsoever.
There is another side to the picture. Either side to the dispute, either labour or management, is given the opportunity to force the appointment of an arbitrator. A stalemate may last for fifteen days and either one or other of the parties may refuse the choice of arbitrator that is named and force the government to name an arbitrator. There may be compulsory principles considered to be in the bill, but I cannot see them.
This morning the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) brought out the point that while there were no penalties in what he considered to be the compulsory part of the bill, in reality penalties were attached to the bill by reason of section 164 of the Criminal Code. One element of effective law is the necessity of imposing penalties. Most hon. members know that in private life I am a clergyman. I am one of those clergymen who believe in hell fire, and I preach it. Sometimes I like to warn people lest they go there, and on certain occasions I feel like telling people to go there. I never have told anyone to go there, but sometimes I feel like telling the government to go there.
Supposing I should get up on a Sunday morning and preach a sermon and tried to be so effective that the congregation would smell the brimstone? Suppose in conclusion I said, "It is all right, I have preached this hell fire but you do not have to worry because nobody is going there anyway." What sort of a preacher would I be if I did that? There would be no sense in that sermon.

That is perhaps one of the cleverest retorts I have heard in this house for a long time-there would be no cents in the collection. Certainly if a preacher preached like that he would not deserve to have any dollars on the plate.
I think my group would be in favour of our being sure that there are no compulsory elements in this bill and the penalties described by the leader of the opposition in section 164 of the Criminal Code could well be done away with. When the proper time

I believe that some limit should be provided in section 5 with regard to the duration of the period of time any agreements decided by the arbitrator would operate. I do not think I can add much more. We are against compulsory bargaining. We are one hundred per cent for the principle of free collective bargaining. We do not believe that the present bill interferes with that principle.
One feature of the bill is that it deals only with this special emergency. If there were a war on, such as we experienced a few years ago, I feel sure we would be ready to support a measure of conscription such as was brought down in the last war. That would be compulsion in a national emergency. I repeat that I cannot see any compulsory features about this legislation. Another point I should like to make is that the present bill does not apply to our labour legislation; it is applicable only to the present state of emergency. It will not affect any labour relations or legislation of the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as other members who have taken part previously in this debate have emphasized, this is indeed a most urgent situation affecting all sections of the people of this nation. It certainly is urgent to the farmers of western Canada as I know it is to agriculture from one end of the nation to the other. It is not only necessary that we have the transportation system operating in order to move our grain and livestock products but it is even more urgent in order that we may have supplies of gasoline and repair parts in order to take off the present harvest. I believe the farmers feel that the stoppage in railway operations should come to a halt immediately. Not only that, they feel that adequate steps should be taken so that such a situation will not come to pass at any time in the future.
I might say that some people in Canada felt that, after the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) had announced the calling of parliament immediately, parliament would have been called within forty-eight hours. Apparently even the T.C.A. official who talked to me thought so. He assured me that parliament was opening last Wednesday and that other members were making reservations. Therefore I made a reservation for Tuesday night and arrived here last Wednesday. While the railway strike is very urgent so far as the average farmer is concerned, it was even more urgent in my case because I left what I hope will prove to be a reasonably good crop.
_ I am speaking at this time partly because it has been reported in various newspapers


from time to time within the last few days that there was a -clear division in the C.C.F. party, that there were members of the party representing farming constituencies who believed that the position of the railroad unions was unreasonable. I wish to deal with that contention in a few words.
It seems to me one of the basic causes of the strike is the fact that the government removed price controls in what I would call a disorderly rush. The cost of living of the workers is going up almost every day, and they feel that in order to protect the standard of living of themselves and their families something has to be done. But as far as the present inflationary situation is concerned, it affects farmers in exactly the same way. Their costs of production are going up almost daily, while the prices of a great many of our primary products are falling.
The farmers know that our railway system is very important and must be kept in operation at all times. But they also know that every time the railways go to the board of transport commissioners asking for an increase in freight rates, they are given an increase, and in a discriminatory manner. The railways obtain everything they ask from the board of transport commissioners. The workers see railway profits increasing rapidly, while their own standard of living is going down. As a result they believe action must be taken if they are to feed and clothe and house their families properly. For instance, in April of 1950 the net revenue of the C.P.R. showed an increase of 103 per cent as compared with the same month in 1949. The increase in May was 130 per cent, and in June 206 per cent. The Canadian National net to June, 1950, was $60,500,000, as compared to $950,000 for the same period last year. The truth is that the railways have never been in a better position to pay the workers reasonable wages. As has been pointed out already, the people now on strike are the lower paid groups employed by the railways, whose wages are a good deal lower than those paid in other comparable industries.
I believe that the position of the farmers and the position of the workers across this country are identical at this time. I do not think legislation which is fair to one is necessarily unfair to the other. The Saskatchewan farmers' union has circulated a letter signed by its president, J. L. Phelps, setting forth the position of that organization with respect to the present railway strike, from which I should like to read one paragraph:
We feel the present situation has developed because proper policies were not adopted to provide the necessary stability. We believe that bold and decisive action must be taken by our government immediately. The Saskatchewan farmers' union

therefore urge, in the strongest possible terms, your immediate consideration for submitting a plan to the members of the House of Commons now summoned for a special session in order to lay before them a proposal to establish immediately a price stabilization commission, upon which industry, labour and farmers will be adequately and proportionately represented. The duty of this price stabilization commission would be to proceed at once to fix the prices of manufactured goods, wages, hours, rents, profits and the price of primary products, including those of agriculture used for Canadian consumption, in fair relationship one to the other, and that this price stabilization commission be further charged with the responsibility of revising, from time to time, prices for the purpose of eliminating any inequalities as well gs making the necessary adjustments resulting from technological changes.
I agree with the sentiments expressed in that paragraph. If we are to have industrial peace, if the farmers of Canada are to continue all-out production, then each must receive a fair return. But of course there must be some control; otherwise strikes will continue, and there will be unrest in agriculture.
I find that I cannot support the bill the government has presented to parliament. As I .see it that bill contains two main points. First, the workers on the railways are ordered back; then compulsory arbitration is provided. I believe that at this time the workers must be ordered back, but I disagree with the provisions of the bill concerning compulsory arbitration. As an alternative to this bill we have moved an amendment to the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). By that amendment the workers would not be given everything for which they have asked; they would be merely guaranteed the concessions offered by the railroads pending free negotiation. I believe the workers would accept such a proposition and go back to work with good spirit, to operate the railways efficiently as they have in the past. The other matters would be left to negotiation.
I do hope, Mr. Speaker, this parliament will do nothing at this time to take away any of the hard-won freedom now enjoyed by the workers, the producers, or any other group in the nation. I believe the members of this house would be well advised to support the C.C.F. alternative.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a word before the vote is taken. It is not my intention to hold up the house unnecessarily, but I think I should have something to say on this subject. In the first place, in my view the responsibility of necessity must lie with the government. It seems to me that if the government had fully realized the seriousness of the situation they would have acted a long time before they did. I believe it is the consensus of opinion
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act that the railways must be put back into operation immediately, so that the entire economy of Canada may not be dislocated. There is no doubt that practically every portion of that economy is feeling the effects of this strike, this tie-up of the railways. I hesitate to use the words "by this strike" because some might take it that I am against the strike. Let me make it abundantly clear, Mr. Speaker, that I believe labour should have the right to strike; that is the only weapon labour has against industry. For that reason alone I maintain that the power to strike should never be taken away from the unions. But there is great economic difficulty facing all classes of the Canadian people. This has been referred to before but I believe it is worth repeating.
Agriculture, particularly in the west, will be seriously affected by this tie-up. The time is coming, in fact it is at hand, when the crops must be harvested. If there is a shortage of gasoline for power it might result in the destruction of many bushels of wheat. Then again there are not the storage facilities on the farms to take care of the forthcoming crop; that is one phase of the difficulties which face us. There are other phases which apply to almost every part of our economy one could mention. Many people are suffering from unemployment because of this strike. The railways are just as much to blame as are the unions.
At this particular time, Mr. Speaker, I should mention one of the transportation systems which is doing a worth-while job, and that is the trucking industry. On several other occasions I have spoken in this house about the trucking industry, pointing out the necessity of having a healthy trucking organization to take care of transportation problems. I think it would be well for the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to note on this occasion the outstanding part the trucking industry is playing in conveying necessary goods, and particularly those goods necessary to our defence forces so that those boys who have offered their lives in the defence of this country can be properly trained. The trucking industry is also playing an outstanding part in delivering drugs to all parts of Canada where they are needed. I believe the trucking industry as a whole should be commended for the worth-while part they are playing in the economy of this country.
I said a moment ago that the unions and the men involved cannot be expected to carry the full responsibility for the consequences of this strike, and one has only to recall that the government itself is responsible in large measure for having permitted the cost of living to rise to such heights. When we

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act found freight rates going up there was no concerted effort on the part of the government to see that prices were maintained at a level which would not unduly affect the economy of the country. When one finds that the cost of living is rising on every hand, not because of anything done by the ordinary workingman, then one must expect there is going to be economic dislocation. The men who are suffering because of this increased cost of living will have to do something to counteract it, and the only thing that labour can do under those circumstances is to ask for an increase in pay. These members of the non-operating unions who are now asking for increased wages are the people who were suffering because they did not have sufficient income to meet rising costs. The railway unions are not the only ones affected by these rising costs. Every workingman in Canada is affected by them, yet the government sits idly by and does nothing to help these people provide a decent standard of living for their families. Since that is the direct responsibility of the government, then the government must take by far the greatest share of the blame. Let us not condemn these people who are taking part in the strike as the ones who are causing the increases in costs.
May I say just a word, Mr. Speaker, about the new president of the Canadian National Railways, Mr. Donald Gordon. In my view Mr. Gordon is a very capable executive. He served as chairman of the prices board during the war. In that position he was-I was going to say he was practically a dictator. In that capacity he did a fairly good job. As one of the members just indicated, he learned some bad habits in that position. I am not so sure, Mr. Speaker, that the government would not be well advised, in any further negotiations between the railways and the unions, to substitute someone else for Mr. Gordon. I believe it is quite clear that the unions are not prepared to conduct further negotiations with Mr. Gordon as head of the railway company. I am not speaking disparagingly at all of Mr. Gordon, but I believe it would help negotiations if the government could appoint someone else as negotiator.
I should like to refer to the bill for just a moment, and then to the amendment and subamendment. The leader of this party has stated that, in general, we would accept the bill. He certainly never indicated he would accept all the clauses. It will be necessary, as discussion of the bill progresses, to make certain amendments here and there to the various sections of the bill. I wish to say a word about the amendment. In my judgment


the amendment does not solve the problem at all. Let me read it to you:
That Bill No. 1 be not now read the second time but that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given to a measure which would provide for the appointment of a national administrator to ensure immediate operation of the railways pending final solution of the dispute by the free process of collective bargaining.
This amendment provides for two things. First, it provides that there shall be a national administrator. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that there are some of the local unions across Canada that are not in favour of a national administrator. I do not say that applies to the heads of the unions, but there are some of the local unions throughout this country that are not in favour of a national administrator. The other objection I have to the amendment is that there is no finality to it. True, a national administrator would be appointed, but there is no provision that agreement shall be arrived at by a certain time. In effect it means that if a national administrator is appointed the unions will be forced to continue under their present agreement without any increase in pay, and that negotiations could be continued for the next ten years. It offers no solution.
When this bill was introduced it was the unanimous opinion of the house that the railways should be put into operation immediately and negotiations reopened, with some hope that there would be a finality to those negotiations. I want to make it clear once more that this party is entirely in accord with collective bargaining. If we can accept the Prime Minister's word, and I think we can, as being sincere when he said during the introduction of this bill that this would not be a precedent but was only to apply to this emergency, then I think we could not say in the strict sense of the term-and I use that word advisedly-that it is compulsory legislation; because without doubt I am against compulsory legislation.
If I may just refer to the subamendment for a moment, I would say this, Mr. Speaker. I think that the subamendment is put in in the wrong place. I do not see how it can very well fit in with the amendment, because the amendment calls for an administrator, not an arbitrator; and under the subamendment you are making the administrator in effect an arbitrator, something which was not intended, I take it, by the mover of the amendment in the Conservative party. I cannot say that I am in any disagreement with any of the points which are indicated in the subamendment other than the last one, and that may have been an oversight. Let me read the last one for you: "the check-off of

trade union dues." I think the intention of the mover of the subamendment was a voluntary check-off. If that is so, then I could agree with that. But if it is a compulsory check-off I could not agree with it.

But the leader of this party, when he was speaking, indicated to you, Mr. Speaker, that even though Bill No. 1 will be passed, it will not be a solution to our problem. It will not be a solution to our economic problem, to the strike problem or to any of those problems which will arise between labour and management in any industry. It seems to me that we should be occupying ourselves on this occasion with legislation which would tend to do away with the necessity of strikes in the future. We must devise some means of raising the standard of living of the people of this country instead of having costs continually rise, because that will not settle the matter. I do not intend to delve into that

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason we are here today is to find some vehicle or method by which to get the railways back into operation and certainly not for the purpose of writing a union agreement. I think that we should all bear that fact in mind and keep that as our aim so long as these discussions continue here in this house. However, that point has been overlooked to a considerable degree, and the discussion has gone at some length into the matter of the clauses which should appear in an agreement. I therefore found that I was in a position calling for a statement of my stand in this case. If the discussion had not gone so far afield I would not have risen. Certainly I had not intended to rise and had not prepared a speech for this occasion. I have, however, made some few notes, and I will refer to them, although they may not be in order and my speech may be somewhat rambling, as some of the previous ones have been.
I say that we did not come here to write an agreement or to make an agreement because I know that the railway men whom we represent-and there are railway men in a great many constituencies-do not want us or expect us to write an agreement. They wish us, as early as possible, to find some method by which the wheels may again begin to turn. I attended a meeting of striking employees and requested certain information regarding rates of pay, et cetera. I knew that their rates of pay were, in most cases, out of line with those in other industries, particularly the industries in the area in which I live. However, I asked for that certain information and they were reluctant to give it to me as one who was going to discuss their affairs. Their reason was not that they felt that their rates did compare favourably with the rates in other industries but rather that they did not wish to have the discussion brought to the floor of the house. They were afraid, as many others have been, that a discussion of the kind would be carried on in the house to such an extent that action would be delayed providing for their return to work.
I mentioned the comparative rates of pay, and I wish to refer to them further. It is not true that the railway workers are a highly paid class. That is a fallacy that has been

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act perpetuated, possibly, I believe, because the running trades receive large pay cheques quite regularly. But that is so not because of their high rates of pay but because of the long hours which they spend on the road. Their rates of pay do not compare, as a basic rate, with anything in industry; that is, they may compare but certainly not too favourably with the logging and mining industry. They are somewhat below. That is a fallacy that will have to be remembered by the members of this house; because I understand the negotiations are coming up in the near future for that particular group of employees. In my opinion the rates of pay of the striking employees are below the average of all industries in Canada. I feel that their case is perfectly justified; and certainly I am prepared to back their demands in every way possible. But, as I said before, it was not our responsibility in this house.
The responsibility for calling a strike is a very grave one. I recognize the strain that the heads of these large unions were under, and the responsibility which they shared at the time they had to call this strike. I am sure they did it because they felt they were acting in the best interests of those whom they represent, and because they had obtained a very large majority, somewhere in the neighbourhood of 97 per cent, in favour of such action, a circumstance which could not be ignored.
It has been said that the method of taking the ballot was undemocratic. I do not agree with that statement. Because the membership extended from coast to coast it would have been very difficult to supervise a strike ballot unless there was some identification of who was marking his "x" on the ballot. It was pointed out to me at the meeting of the strikers that no one in that particular area knew how anyone voted, and the ballot was not taken in that way for that purpose. It was not taken in that way for the purpose of influencing the outcome of the ballot. However, I might say that if the ballot had been absolutely secret, in view of the fact that 97 per cent of the workers voted in this way, there is no doubt that a sufficiently large majority would have been obtained to warrant calling the strike.
There is another matter, namely, the matter of negotiation on the part of the companies, to which I should like to refer. I have said also that improvements could be made in the way the negotiations were handled. However, the companies are responsible for choosing their negotiator. It is no business of the unions whom the companies choose. It is the companies' responsibility. If they do not choose one who they feel is a good negotiator, then it is the companies' loss.

Good negotiators are picked not for the purpose of giving something to the union. Good negotiators are picked for the purpose of maintaining the best interests of the companies. I have not heard of any statement by the union negotiators that the company negotiator should be changed or that they did not wish to negotiate further with him.
Let me return to the bill itself. Although certain officials of the union may not agree with me, I believe that the employees in my particular area are very anxious that this thing be settled, or at least that they get back to work and that negotiations be resumed. That was my impression while attending their meeting. Certainly they did not indicate that they wished to go back to work without any assurance of improvement, but they feel that they should get back to work at the earliest possible moment and that negotiations should be resumed as soon as possible. Therefore I am prepared to support the bill introduced by the government, with some reluctance, however, regarding section 5. The fact that the railway unions are allowed to go on strike, to use that very strong economic weapon, is some reassurance. To shut the railways down for a week is to use a very grave economic weapon, and it is still maintained. Once this dispute is settled this bill will be no longer effective. Should the unions desire to negotiate another year, and if we were to take the stand that the unions could not go on strike again, we would have to call parliament and possibly go through the same procedure-the Lord forbid, I may say. But there is the possibility; and certainly parliament could not be called any earlier than it has been on this occasion. Therefore the workers would still have their right to the economic weapon that they enjoy at the present time.
In the words of the Prime Minister, the amendment introduced by the leader of the opposition is not worthy of consideration. Because the subamendment is tied to it, it is also unworthy of consideration. The unions do not want the government to negotiate an agreement. I am sure that is a factual statement. To introduce new clauses in dispute now would be indeed unfair. The one particular clause that I have in mind, which has been introduced by the C.C.F. party, is the matter of check-off of union dues.

I would refer first to the statement made by my leader in opening, that as far as either party to the dispute was concerned, with such restraint as we may be able to exercise, we should avoid saying anything which might lead to future controversy. But I must say

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act that I regret the attack that was made here upon Mr. Donald Gordon. I say that because I am unable to appreciate any attack of that sort on anyone who has no opportunity of answering. I add that I am utterly opposed to condemning anyone on such loose reports as we have of the negotiations which have taken place to date. It seems to me it is nothing but the old cry, "Crucify him," in so far as we have the facts here. I have no prejudices for or against Mr. Gordon. Perhaps if I had any they would be against him, because I am one of those persons who have been compelled to bear the terrific strain of listening to him sing. If we are to be influenced to comment in any way I want to say that Mr. Gordon may have abruptly terminated these negotiations. As to that none of us know, but I do know that the negotiating committee for the men refused the offer of our own Prime Minister for a thirty-day respite.
I should like to say that I am going to vote for this bill. I am adopting a strange course; at least, to me it is strange. I believe the speech of our leader. this morning was one of the most masterly speeches to which I have listened in this House of Commons. I agreed with every word of it. Now that the amendment which he proposed is gone-of course I supported it-I find myself in the position where the paramount issue is to get these wheels rolling as quickly as possible. I loathe and despise some of the provisions in this bill. To our shame let it be said that we have contributed nothing towards the permanent solution of our problems, but since the amendments are gone there is nothing left for me but to support the only way of getting these wheels moving. I am not in disagreement with the criticisms of this bill but I believe the situation is so fraught with danger that I could not forgive myself, even in the face of criticism by uninformed people, if by my vote I contributed in any way to retarding the operation of these railways.
It has not been suggested to me by anyone but I know full well that I could have found it convenient to be absent at this particular time. I conclude by saying that it is not a crime for one to vote against his party. I believe perhaps we have had an occasion today upon which more than a few of us might have done so. If that be a party crime, I am guilty. If it is not I stand here and say that, as an expedient to get these railways operating, I intend to vote for this bill because that is the only sure way of which I know to have these trains "operating by tomorrow or the following day. I am mindful of the fact that in the province from which I come six hundred oil wells are closed today, and nearly


all drilling operations are going to be closed owing to a lack of steel pipe. I know that with a crop ripening in the west there is not enough gasoline in the country, and certainly not in the province of Alberta, to harvest this crop. I know that if this grain is dumped on the ground the excess moisture we have in my province will cause it to sprout, and in no time it will start to rot. I am therefore forsaking a principle for which I have long fought, but I do that as an expedient and with a clear conscience that at least we will be sure our economy will continue to function.
