I shall only detain the house for a minute or two in order to make my position clear with respect to the forthcoming vote. In common with my colleague who has just resumed his seat, I listened to the most masterly discourse on any subject to which I have listened in over twelve sessions in this House of Commons during my leader's presentation this morning. I believe he proposed an excellent amendment. I am not satisfied with this bill as it is, nor am I satisfied with the actions of the government. Several ministers have indicated that they expected this strike to take place. If the government as a whole expected it and did not wish to take the proper steps themselves but wished to refer the matter to parliament, in my opinion parliament should have been assembled on the day the strike was to take place. I feel strongly about that, Mr. Speaker.
The vast majority of Canadian citizens are anxious to see this strike ended and to have our great transportation, systems functioning again. The people are also anxious to have some assurance that this situation shall not be repeated in the near future. The bill contains no provision to ensure that, so the people will be disappointed. I shall tell you why I am voting for the bill. It is due to the fact that I know something about the agricultural problems of this country. I can tell you that while all the citizens of Canada are suffering as a result of this strike, in the west we have one harvest a year and that is now taking place. In some parts of the prairies the grain is spoiling because of this strike. For ninety per cent of the people in the west this grain represents their living.
I have a comparison of my own which I should like to make. In 1942 I fought what I thought was a silly plebiscite. When the government of the day carried it I went out in my riding and did everything humanly possible to assist in obtaining the largest percentage of yes votes in any riding in Canada. That is the way I feel about this

matter. Since we have a tremendous government majority, elected under an outdated electoral system, and we have done all we can to improve this bill, although it is still not satisfactory to me I am going to be forced conscientiously to vote for it. In order to get this strike ended and the transportation system functioning, I shall vote for the measure. I hope I shall not be misunderstood in this matter, Mr. Speaker. I believe in the party system of government and a strong official opposition, but having done all we can to improve this measure I must take this stand at this time.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we came down here to do one thing, namely to get turning again the wheels of industry which are dependent upon the operation of the railways. I object as strenuously as does any other member of this house to compulsion of any sort in labour-management disputes or in anything that has to do with collective bargaining. There comes a time, however, when, under the democratic principle of the greatest good for the greatest number, we must decide whether, despite the principle involved, we are going to support a measure which will have the effect of starting industry again or are going to hold it up and by so doing compel-and I use the word "compel"-many thousands of others to lose their livelihood because of their dependence upon the railways. Before the house disposes of the amendment moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce I should like to say a brief word about it. I think all of us welcome the introduction of that amendment by the Prime Minister. Many of us think that it should have been announced at an earlier time. It all goes back to the fact that this is very hastily drafted and hastily conceived legislation. In fairness to the house, I think the Prime Minister ought to have made known his willingness to introduce such an amendment at a much earlier stage of the proceedings. He has introduced it and we welcome it. We welcome it because it at least has the virtue that it confines within a narrower sphere the dubious principle of compulsory

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act arbitration, the thing in this bill which has incurred the opposition of a number of us on this side of the house. To the extent that it narrows the application of a vicious principle we welcome it.
I think that one must pause for a moment to consider the position in which the arbitrator is going to find himself with reference to some of the features of the dispute which at first blush may not be those that hon. members might consider most difficult. I think the section under consideration should be read along with the third paragraph of the preamble. That paragraph seems to treat the subject matter of the dispute as being confined simply to hours and wage rates. It reads:
And whereas the railway companies and the bargaining agents of the employees appear to have agreed that existing wage rates should be increased, and the forty-hour week introduced but appear to have been unable to agree as to the amount and effective date of the wage increase or the date at which the forty-hour week would be effective and the terms and conditions upon which it would be introduced.
The Prime Minister will recall that there were other factors as well in the dispute. At the concluding conference between the parties, as I understand it, there was a suggestion that some of these other issues should be reserved for further negotiation; the Prime Minister recalls those to which I allude. It seems to me that the arbitrator, who will be called upon to perform a very difficult task, should have some clear direction in the bill as to the extent of his duties in reference to those other conditions. If he reads the third paragraph of the preamble as qualifying the intent of section 5 of the bill he may consider that he is confined to the two subjects of hours and wages, and some further dispute may arise as to the interpretation of this act as it applies to those other subjects in dispute. In fairness to the arbitrator, and certainly in fairness to the parties to the dispute, I would urge that any possibility of further misunderstanding between the parties be eliminated at this point.

In my view it is not
possible for this committee at this time to make an exact statement of the position of the proposals when the negotiations were broken off. However, a statement was issued on Saturday evening by the press bureaux of the railway companies, which was included by the Minister of Labour in his recital of the facts last evening. I do not know whether that statement would conform with the recollection or admissions of the negotiating committee for the men, but one statement was to the effect that there should be an agreement along lines indicated by the

negotiating committee as satisfactory, to negotiate amendments in connection with certain rules. That is a part of what was apparently contained in the proposals that were being discussed in the hope of arriving at a collective bargain; an agreement along lines indicated as satisfactory by the negotiating committee, to negotiate amendments in connection with certain rules. That is why the amendment to section 5 which is now suggested was drawn in this way. If there is any dispute, unfortunately the arbitrator will have to satisfy his own mind as to the gap which still existed at that time.

I think all hon. members
will wish to give the arbitrator, in the discharge of his difficult task, the utmost possible help, in the directions to be contained in this legislation. The third paragraph of the preamble at first blush seems to treat the matters at issue between the parties as being confined to those two, namely, hours and rates of wages.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE

There is one other matter not referred to in the third paragraph, and which is not included in the information I have gathered from press statements as to the position of affairs at the time negotiations were broken off. According to the press statements apparently there was not at that time discussion as to whether or not there would be a check-off. That seemed to have disappeared from the area of discussion, though it had been there at some earlier date. I do not know whether it had been dropped or whether it was just being left in abeyance, to be taken up after the other matters were decided. That is something about which the arbitrator would have to satisfy himself. He would have to be satisfied as to whether it was still in dispute between the parties or whether it had been dropped. All the other matters would be covered by the general language of paragraph 3, the terms and conditions upon which the forty-hour week would be introduced; it is all implied in that, as far as my information goes. Personally, if I were acting as arbitrator and were shown that the statement published in the newspapers was really handed out by the negotiators for the railways -I think it has the mimeographed signature of the press bureaux of the railway companies -I would take it as a statement by which the railways were bound, and would take it as saying that at that point their offers contained everything mentioned in that statement. It also purports to say what was the position of the negotiating committee for the men at that moment. I would not be prepared, without confirmation from the men, to

take that statement as indicating their position. I would feel that I had to get from the men a statement of their position at that time. It has been referred to in declarations that were made, or that were published by the newspapers as coming from some of them, but that is something which would have to be determined.
With respect to the position 6f the railways, I should not think the arbitrator would be apt to have very much difficulty, because this statement was put out at that time apparently by the press bureaux of the companies. I should imagine it would not have been put out if it had not indicated the real position being taken by the representatives of the railways at that moment. I do not mean they were saying, "We have arrived at a point where we have agreed on all these things." They were taking parts of what they wanted in the over-all agreement, but certainly it would indicate the proposals they were making for a collective agreement at that moment.

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act
The fact that the Prime Minister referred to the statements made by the railways last Saturday night, Mr. Chairman, raises another question. It concerns the whole question of the limiting new subsection 3 moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the reference to the hotel and water transport workers. Deliberately some of us have not referred to that question at all throughout this debate because we took it, at least I did, from the terms of the bill that it applied equally to all the employees involved in the present dispute. "Employee" is defined as an employee of a railway company, and "railway company" is defined as any of the companies listed in a certain schedule. This schedule includes hotel and steamship companies and railways that own steamship companies and hotels. I point out that one of the statements made by the railways on Saturday night concerning the position they had reached is as follows:
Hotel and water transport workers to be covered in a separate contract for one year to be granted an increase of two cents per hour effective September 1, 1950.
That may have been the position reached by the companies that night, but it certainly was not acceptable to the unions. The Prime Minister now says that this new paragraph calls for arbitration between the limits established by the differences between them on Saturday night, but I thought the government's bill dealt with that point. The government's bill made it clear, I thought, that whatever kind of agreement as to wages, as to the effective date of the forty-hour week and the length of the agreement, is made, it will be the same for all unions involved.

I am sure the bill is unpalatable, and I am sure that the Prime Minister is quite correct when he said he had no firm view because amendments were being made yesterday, a further amendment is being made today, and if this debate continued for any length of time I am satisfied that, owing to representations from outside the house from one side or the other, there would be further amendments to this bill. This section is one which could be left out and the results obtained by getting the men back to work and resuming operations of the railroad, while letting collective bargaining operate in the ordinary way between management and the great railway organizations that have been dealing with each other with great success for decades in this country.
The amendment now before us is simply a further attempt to carry new principles into legislation which at some future date may operate as a precedent, and those who find that being done will regard it as very unsatisfactory indeed. This section neither assures to the Canadian public the continued operation of the railroads in the months and years ahead, nor does it assure the workers

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act
the basic right of collective bargaining, upon which good will and co-operation must depend, no matter what temporary arrangements are made. Obviously the bill will pass in its present form from the indications of support the government has received. I wish to make it quite clear that I regard it as something that is not only unsatisfactory to those directly affected by the limitation imposed by this section on the long-established principle of collective bargaining; it is also unsatisfactory to the people of Canada because the bill offers no assurance that this will not happen again. It offers to the workers none of the assurances that their rights are going to be protected in the years ahead.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, because of the impatience of the private members on the government side of the house, what I have to say is for their benefit. I am glad that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made the point about the powers of the arbitrator to set different rates of wages for groups for which the bargaining committee was asking a similar rate, and also for setting a different time for the expiry of any collective agreements that might be entered into. It seems to me that the chairman of the Canadian National Railways was trying to separate some of the unions from the larger bargaining group and make separate agreements with them.
The purpose of a trade union is to improve the bargaining strength of individuals by collecting them together into one organization. Another means of increasing the bargaining strength is by bringing various unions into one organization for bargaining purposes. It is quite clear that in the recent negotiations the purpose of the Canadian National Railway Company was to separate these unions so that they could make a separate agreement with each of them, having the agreements expire at different times so that never again could the railway employees confront the company with a united front of all agreements expiring at the same time.
I should like to point out to the few members on the government side who claim to be union men and to those who are representing trade union or workers' constituencies that the powers that are now given to the arbitrator are, either wittingly or unwittingly, designed to weaken the trade union movement for collective bargaining purposes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: This is the section upon which this party, through its leader, took its strongest stand. As we see it, this section represents the most direct move ever made in any country-

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Yes, in spite of what the Prime Minister said last evening, this section represents the most direct move ever made in any country to set up provisions for an arbitrator in a labour dispute with absolute power to determine. This is a terrific power to place in the hands of one man. It is a power unequalled in its amplitude in any other country having the democratic concept of government. There is no one in this parliament who at any time did not wish to give support to the assurance in our country of continued railway transportation. That was and is our attitude. No one had objection to paragraphs 1 and 2, and to the noble preamble. What is being done in this section of the bill is what we take our objection to, namely the granting of uncontrolled and untrammelled power to one person to determine decisions in trade union matters and to change the provisions for settlement of labour disputes that have existed for over seventy years.
I believe that if the debates that have taken place on this bill lead to the setting up in parliament of a committee to re-examine and restate the principles of collective bargaining, much good will result in labour relations. Evolution makes change necessary. When the Prime Minister endeavours to say that this section does not mean compulsory arbitration, I say that it means nothing else and that it means a change in this country that will create a precedent from which in future relations there may be no departure. It was to preserve the principles of collective bargaining that the leader of the opposition moved the amendment to settle this strike by collective bargaining rather than resort to a provision which is dangerous in its import and dangerous in the absolute power that it confers on one human being.
As it now stands this section grants such absolute power as has never been granted before, and I say that in spite of what the Prime Minister said in reference to Britain, because I have that legislation before me. The principle enunciated in this section is one that in the future will constitute a precedent; and the pathway of today will be the highway of tomorrow. It is dangerous in its import to the continuance of collective bargaining and that relationship which, in my opinion, should prevail as between management and labour. There is no use in endeavouring to ask that this section be not continued as it now is in this bill; but it is sections such as that, passed under urgency, which so often lead to tyranny. Urgency there has been for months. While the urgency
74

Maintenance of Railway Operation Act of the situation required action by this government and while our economic position in this country was worsening week by week, the government was vacationing. The record that was placed before this house last evening by the Minister of Labour shows that for days in August the government did nothing. The government was not giving that leadership which the people of Canada had a right to expect. Having vacillated and having been inactive for months the government now introduces a section such as section 5 because of the present urgency of the situation; and urgent it is. In my own province the situation is as serious as it is in any other part of this country. Because of that urgency which, in considerable measure, is due to lack of action on the part of this government, a section such as section 5 is now passed. It will be carried. But from this day on collective bargaining will be an instrument which may become only a memory.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
I should like to say a word on this principle of free collective bargaining that the Conservative spokesmen have been attacking. In my speech a little while ago I claimed that this bill did not really propose any compulsion. The thirty-day clause, together with a longer period, fixed by order in council if necessary, gives the right of free collective bargaining and places the responsibility of free collective bargaining upon the two contending parties. It is only when they themselves have failed through free collective bargaining to reach an agreement than an arbitrator is appointed.
What I would like to ask my Conservative friends, because the problem is in my mind, is this: They believe in free collective bargaining; so do we, so does the government, so do our C.C.F. friends. But when free collective bargaining has failed, what is their proposal?

speechtext: They have not any.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: All this bill proposes is that when free collective bargaining has failed an arbitrator is appointed to settle the point.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
We welcome the amendment which the Prime Minister proposed to clause 5; but one of the most contentious points raised in this entire discussion is the question of the status of the two groups of workers, namely, hotel employees and water transport workers. The unions have been seeking to secure for them exactly the same terms of settlement that they got for the other unions. By reason of the clause which refers to the four cents it was hoped that that point had been conceded to the unions. Actually I find that the leaders of the unions who were negotiating this matter felt that

they had at least won that one point when this bill was circulated last night.
They felt that one of the points this bill gave them was that there was to be no distinction between the treatment accorded the hotel and water transport workers and that accorded to other unions. According to the Prime Minister's statement, that is not so. I would suggest that the Prime Minister give consideration to removing from the sphere of negotiation which the arbitrator would deal with the question relating to the ten points, and that this bill provide for the same treatment on the part of the water transport workers and hotel workers as for the other unions. As long as there is that distinction this bill will not be satisfactory to the railway workers. While they may obey the law and go back to work, it will not be with good grace if it should happen that a different settlement is awarded to the two groups I have mentioned from that awarded to the other group.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
May I also join in the suggestion that this particular point should be reconsidered? The unions that have been negotiating have been negotiating as a unit, and have endeavoured to operate that way throughout. Anything which tended to break that unity would, I am perfectly sure, be resented by the larger group of unions.
As a matter of fact, when suggestions were made during negotiations that they should get less than the larger unions, the larger unions felt that they must insist on the same treatment for those smaller people as for themselves. I am sure they would deeply resent any differentiation, and it would just be another case of unrest and discontent.
There is a certain amount of loyalty among these union members who have been working together through their groups. They would have felt, I am sure, that to accept for themselves an agreement which separated in any way the smaller group of workers would have been disloyalty to that group. The government would be well advised to consider this small group of people as coming under any of the decisions that are beneficial to the larger unions.
I have heard it said that the railway management considered throughout that after all this was a minor matter. In fact on one occasion I heard it described as peanuts. If for the sake of a small part of the negotiating unions we fail to do what is justice to them, and give the larger unions the feeling that this group which has relied on them has been discriminated against, I think it will tend to create bad public relations and bad union relations in the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: They are not being discriminated against in any way. The government, in the bill which it recommended to parliament, has treated them in the same way as the other unions, namely, as one unit; and everything that binds the arbitrator with respect to any one binds him as much with respect to those two small groups as it does to the others. Therefore the arbitrator will have to investigate the disputes between the parties; but so that there might be no suggestion that his powers will enable him to reverse that decision, he cannot reverse the decision. Everything that is bound by the statute is bound for everybody, but what is open to further negotiation between the parties are the things that are in dispute between them. It may be that they would agree on different terms of contracts or on different arrangements. If they could not agree the arbitrator would have to make a finding; but he would have before him an example of the recommendations to the government and of the action of parliament in recognizing the desirability of not doing anything that would make anyone feel that he was being disloyal to a comrade.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: Let us have this clear. The Prime Minister just said that the arbitrator is bound in his dealings with the hotel and water transport workers in the same way as in his dealings with the others. But is it clear that, if the parties do not agree to the same kind of settlement for both, he has the power under this act, if he so decides in his wisdom, or otherwise, to award a different wage increase to one group than to the other, and a different date for the forty-hour week for one group than for the other, and a different period of time for the length of contract between the two groups?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE

I would not like to discuss those details; but in the recommendation we made to parliament and in the bill itself we have attempted to treat as one unit all those involved in this dispute. On all of the points in which we have provided expressly, we have stated the arbitrator cannot undo what we are doing. On the other matters he will have to make a determination as to the extent of the gap and the bridging of the gap.
For instance, I would not like to give any opinion as a lawyer as to whether or not in the position taken by the parties at the last moment there would still be room for the arbitrator to say that one group, perhaps the car men, would get one rate, and another group, perhaps the boilermakers, would get another. I do not know. We have endeavoured to treat the whole group who are out, 69262-6J
Maintenance of Railway Operation Act those who have withdrawn from work, as one unit; and our reason for doing so is that we thought it would be unfortunate to ask by legislation that any portion of them should do something which they would regard as disloyal to their comrades.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: Then we can take it that the intention of the legislation is so far as possible to keep the unions as a unit in their negotiations?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext: I would not put it in that way. The intention was not by legislation to require any of the unions to adopt a course that they would regard as disloyal to their fellows.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
Although it was my
privilege to second this morning the amendment proposed by my leader, I purposely refrained from speaking on that occasion in the hope that the deliberations in the house might be shortened, and that we might arrive at a decision at an early hour so as to get these men back to work-because, after all, that is the concern of every Canadian citizen at this time. I cannot help feeling that the discussion that goes on now almost interminably defers that ultimate goal.
However, we have now arrived at the section in the bill which was the cause of the opposition from members in this party. In spite of the fact that the pill has been well sugar-coated by now, I would say it is still bitter, and as the coating wears off it will become more and more bitter. I cannot see how those in the house, regardless of the party leadership they follow, who in their hearts believe in a system of free enterprise, to which we give unlimited lip service, can vote for a section like this which disrupts the management-worker relationships which have been built up in this country over a period of fifty years.
History is not made overnight; negotiations are not broken down overnight. I say to hon. members that it is the first bite that creates the appetite, and that there is being established by section 5 a precedent that may well be written into all future labour negotiations. I do not think there ever was or ever will be a strike in this country that could not, through the services of a clever advocate, have been termed a strike against the people. They could all be construed as such, because there never was a strike that did not in some way hurt someone-even the strikers themselves. They know that.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that by members of this party and by others this section has been termed compulsion; and, regardless of the whitewashing it has received, it is still compulsion. I hold very strong views

I should still have had to vote against the bill and against this section, because I do not believe it is in the best interests of those things for which we.stand. Somewhere no doubt within the confines of the editorial offices they ran amuck and could not find a nice, short word to put in there. Nevertheless I think it will be admitted that in the history of the world other words and other names have been used such as kings, emperors, as well as czars, and which have brought down upon the heads of some countries a certain amount of opprobrium. I do not think you can take any one word and say that every one who might be described by that word was a despot or a criminal.

speechtext: I think one would have to be very unrealistic if he thought that provision of this kind could be enforced by court or police action. I do not think it would be appropriate to say that parliament passes any law that would not be covered by section 164 of the Criminal Code, but to think that that is an effective way of having the will of parliament followed would be most unrealistic in my opinion. We know that when there is a large section of the population involved, as there is here, that measure just will not work. However, I do not think it would be appropriate to exclude the possibility that it might. Section 164 should be read in conjunction with section 1035 which provides that, whenever imprisonment is a penalty under the Criminal Code and a corporation is being prosecuted, the judge has the discretion to impose a fine. I think those provisions should remain applicable because I believe their removal might be looked upon as an implication that this was a law that parliament had no interest in seeing enforced or obeyed. The only practical enforcement of laws of this kind is the weight of public opinion and the desire of all our people to see our democratic institutions function.
